howToRefresh: Ingest the KY History morning email to public/content/raw-briefs/YYYY-MM-DD.md, run npm run parse-briefs, then npm run build (includes build-home-preview). The homepage also re-reads stories.json in the browser.

stories.title: Walker Daniel, Danville’s namesake
stories.summary: Virginia lawyer Walker Daniel laid out the town at Crow’s Station in 1783, served as the District of Kentucky’s first attorney general, and was killed in 1784; the town was named Danville for him in 1787.
stories.quote: Danville is named for Walker Daniel, a young Virginia lawyer who came to central Kentucky in 1781 and laid out the town at Crow’s Station in 1783.

photo.title: Constitution Square State Historic Site, Danville
photo.attribution: Sarah Stierch (Missvain), CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stories.heroDeck: Danville is named for Walker Daniel, a young Virginia lawyer who came to central Kentucky in 1781 and laid out the town at Crow’s Station in 1783.

stories.title: Chambers Site (15Ml109): an upland Mississippian village
stories.summary: On a Marshall County ridgetop above the Middle Fork of Clarks River, the Chambers site was a Mississippian farming village of about six hectares, lived in about AD 1250–1350.
stories.quote: The Chambers site (15Ml109) is a Mississippian village on a ridgetop overlooking the Middle Fork of Clarks River in Marshall County.

photo.title: Clarks River at Clarks River National Wildlife Refuge (photographed 2012); stand-in, since the Chambers site is not public and no photo of it is used
photo.attribution: Andy Eller, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.heroDeck: The Chambers site (15Ml109) is a Mississippian village on a ridgetop overlooking the Middle Fork of Clarks River in Marshall County.

stories.title: Hartford: Fort Hartford on the Rough River
stories.summary: Settled by about 1782 at a ford on the Rough River, Hartford grew from a frontier fort on Gabriel Madison’s Virginia grant into the seat of Ohio County in 1799 and was incorporated in 1808.
stories.quote: Hartford sits on a bluff above the Rough River, a long tributary of the Green River that early settlers called Rough Creek.

photo.title: Ohio County Courthouse on the square in Hartford (photographed 2013)
photo.attribution: Nyttend · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.heroDeck: Hartford sits on a bluff above the Rough River, a long tributary of the Green River that early settlers called Rough Creek.

stories.title: Treaty of Fort McIntosh, 1785
stories.summary: In 1785 at Fort McIntosh, Pennsylvania, U.S. commissioners including George Rogers Clark signed a treaty with Wyandot, Delaware, Ojibwe and Odawa leaders.
stories.quote: In January 1785 American commissioners met Native leaders at Fort McIntosh), a log fort built in 1778 where the Beaver River meets the Ohio, at present Beaver, Pennsylvania.

photo.title: Looking east across the site of Fort McIntosh, Beaver, Pennsylvania (photographed 2009)
photo.attribution: Nyttend · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.heroDeck: In January 1785 American commissioners met Native leaders at Fort McIntosh), a log fort built in 1778 where the Beaver River meets the Ohio, at present Beaver, Pennsylvania.

stories.title: Yahoo Falls: Kentucky’s tallest waterfall
stories.summary: In McCreary County’s Big South Fork, Yahoo Falls drops about 113 feet into a deep rock house. The Forest Service opened it to visitors in the 1960s, and the National Park Service has managed it since 1987.
stories.place: Yahoo Falls, Big South Fork (McCreary County)
stories.quote: Yahoo Falls is a single plunge of about 113 feet on Yahoo Creek in McCreary County, inside the Big South Fork National River and Recreation Area.

photo.title: Yahoo Falls, Big South Fork, McCreary County (photographed 2008)
photo.attribution: Mason Brock · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.heroDeck: Yahoo Falls is a single plunge of about 113 feet on Yahoo Creek in McCreary County, inside the Big South Fork National River and Recreation Area.

layers.name: Fort Boonesborough
layers.blurb: Daniel Boone’s 1775 settlement on the Kentucky River — Capital of the Colony of Transylvania.

photo.attribution: Bubba73 · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

layers.name: Big Bone Lick
layers.blurb: A Pleistocene salt lick where mastodons left bones in the mud — Kentucky’s window on deep time.

photo.title: Big Bone Lick State Park
photo.attribution: Mattguyver · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0

layers.name: Thomas D. Clark Center for Kentucky History
layers.blurb: Flagship Kentucky Historical Society museum, covering more than 12,000 years of the Commonwealth.

photo.title: Thomas D. Clark Center for Kentucky History
photo.attribution: Lee Wright · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0

layers.name: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace
layers.wiki: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historical Park
layers.blurb: The Sinking Spring farm where Lincoln was born in 1809, plus the Knob Creek boyhood unit.

photo.title: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace memorial
photo.attribution: Jon698 · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0

layers.name: Blue Licks Battlefield
layers.wiki: Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park
layers.blurb: August 19, 1782: the last major Revolutionary War battle in Kentucky.

photo.title: Blue Licks Battlefield monument
photo.attribution: Nyttend · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Old Talbott Tavern
layers.blurb: Court Square tavern since the late 1700s — among America’s oldest inns, still a working bourbon bar.

photo.title: Old Talbott Tavern, Bardstown
photo.attribution: Christopher L. Riley · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

layers.name: Goddard Covered Bridge
layers.blurb: White Bridge: a Town-lattice span over Sand Lick Creek, among Kentucky’s surviving covered bridges.

photo.title: Goddard Covered Bridge
photo.attribution: Greg Hume · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

layers.name: Bourbon Iron Works
layers.blurb: Jacob Myers blew in a charcoal blast furnace here in 1791 — munitions for the early Commonwealth.

photo.title: Bourbon Iron Works (Slate Furnace)
photo.attribution: Jeff Bates · HABS / Library of Congress · Public domain

layers.name: The Kentucke Gazette
layers.blurb: Kentucky’s first newspaper, begun August 11, 1787 by John and Fielding Bradford.

photo.title: Kentucke Gazette printing house
photo.attribution: William Henry Perrin / Filson Club · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Cumberland Falls
layers.blurb: The “Niagara of the South,” and one of the few Western Hemisphere places a moonbow can appear.

photo.title: Cumberland Falls
photo.attribution: Aaron Vowels · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0

layers.name: Frankfort Cemetery
layers.blurb: Hilltop rural cemetery (1844) overlooking the capital — Daniel and Rebecca Boone were reinterred here.

photo.title: Frankfort Cemetery
photo.attribution: Sydney Poore & Russell Poore · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

layers.name: Buffalo Trace Distillery
layers.blurb: A Kentucky River distilling campus with late-1700s roots, continuous through Prohibition.

photo.title: Buffalo Trace Distillery
photo.attribution: Kittugwiki · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0
